newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan central bank undermines cabinet authority.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan central bank undermines cabinet authority.

text.p: The refusal by Taiwan's central bank to accept a cabinet planning agency's low 1997 inflation goal indicates the bank is baulking at the cabinet's sometimes-wishful economic forecasts, analysts said on Monday.

They said the latest dispute, coming in the wake of the cabinet's badly over-optimistic forecast for 1996 economic growth, shows the cabinet's weakness as an objective surveyor of Taiwan's struggling economy.

"These conflicts are happening because the central bank is making a prediction while the cabinet is issuing a target," said National Chengchi University economics professor Norman Yin. Nomura Securities economist Amy Huang said the Council for Economic Planning and Development, the cabinet's top economic policymaker, was more hopeful than realistic.

"The council was saying what it hopes the inflation will be, while the central bank replied by saying what the inflation realistically is going to be," Huang said. The central bank, already at odds with the council over money supply targets, vowed on Monday not to yield meekly to the council's 1997 consumer price growth target of 3.0 percent.
Instead, vice central bank governor Hsu Chia-tung reiterated governor Sheu Yuan-dong's 3.31 percent inflation prediction.
Taiwan's consumer price inflation was 3.07 percent in 1996.
Sheu said on Friday that Taiwan's recovery, which has been far slower than the council had predicted, had not progressed enough for the central bank to accept such low CPI growth.

It was the second time in two months that the bank had baulked at the planning council's targets. The central bank in December refused to lower its official "target zone" for growth of the broadest M2 money supply as suggested by the council.
The conflicts also suggest a central bank trying to assert its policymaking independence, analysts said.
"The central bank is stressing that it is the authority in monetary policy and will not be influenced easily by the council," said National Securities economist Lin Kuo-yang.
Some economic experts say the market itself appears to have lost confidence in the council's ability to chart Taiwan's economic outlook with any degree of accuracy.
The council had forecast the economy would recover rapidly in 1996 to attain gross domestic product growth of 6.8 percent following a 1995 slump caused by political tensions with China.
But the economy sagged for most of 1996 and only began to show signs of life in the fourth quarter, causing officials to lower their full-year GDP estimate to 5.7 percent.
Actual GDP figures will be reported in late February.
"The council simply has not been very objective in its evaluation and therefore most in the market believe the central bank's (inflation) prediction will be right," said Lin.
Nomura's Huang scoffed that the council's apparent view that Taiwan could have both higher growth and lower inflation.
"If GDP growth for 1996 was only 5.7 percent and inflation already was 3.07 percent, how can inflation be lowered in 1997 if the economy gets better?" Huang said.
Businesses appeared sceptical as well.
In a poll published on Monday by the council itself, up to 22 percent of local manufacturing executives felt the economy would grow worse, while only 17 percent said it would improve.

The council, on the other hand, predicted on Monday that an economic recovery would deepen on the strength of December's rise in the index of leading business indicators, the fourth consecutive monthly increase.
Private economists have forecast GDP growth of between 5.70 and 6.20 percent for 1997, compared to the latest government forecast of 6.20 percent.
